profile.reading:
This entry is attributed to Duke Libraries, the library system of Duke University, at a location on Telecom Drive in Durham, North Carolina. That street name is notable. Telecom Drive is where Duke's central information technology and network infrastructure sits, distinct from the university's public facing library buildings such as Perkins, Bostock, and Rubenstein on Duke's West Campus. A facility carrying the name Brandaleone Lab for Data and Visualization sounds, on its face, like a user facing space, the kind of room with large display walls, workstations, and consultation hours that research libraries increasingly build to support data science and visualization work for students and faculty. Duke Libraries does operate services of that kind, including data and visualization consultation and drop in office hours, though public library pages describe the program and its staff rather than naming or locating a specific Brandaleone branded room.

The mismatch between a visualization lab's usual public facing purpose and a Telecom Drive address is worth stating plainly rather than glossing over. It is possible that the name attached to this record covers backend computing or storage infrastructure that supports a visualization program housed elsewhere on campus, with the actual servers, storage, and network equipment sited at Duke's central IT facility for reliability and staffing reasons, a common arrangement at research universities where a public lab's front end is nowhere near the equipment room that powers it. It is also possible the address simply reflects how this record was located and tagged rather than the lab's true public entrance or primary location.

What can be said with confidence is that Duke University Libraries is a well resourced academic library system serving one of the country's leading research universities, that it maintains active data services and visualization support for its community, and that Duke's enterprise computing infrastructure, wherever specifically sited, is built and operated by university staff for internal research and administrative use rather than as a commercial or colocation facility open to outside tenants. No square footage, power capacity, or equipment inventory for this specific address has been published by Duke. That is typical of how research universities handle back of house computing space. It gets documented for internal facilities and IT staff who need to maintain it, not marketed the way a commercial data center operator publishes specifications to attract tenants.

IMPORTANT DATA QUALITY FLAG: the registry facility record tied to this operator (osm:node/10567817971, named 'Brandaleone Lab for Data and Visualization', Durham County NC) does not appear to be a computing data center. Direct research on Duke University Libraries' Center for Data and Visualization Sciences confirms the Brandaleone Lab is a research consultation and visualization services space, not a server room or IT infrastructure facility. This appears to be a source-data mistagging, likely because the location name contains the word 'Data.' A genuine Duke Libraries facility exists, the Duke University Library Service Center at 5 Anson Street, Durham NC, opened 2001, but that is a high-density physical book storage repository (30-foot shelving, climate controlled at 50F/30% humidity for 3 million to 15 million volume capacity) for Duke and UNC-Chapel Hill library collections, also not a computing data center. No evidence was found of an actual server/IT data center operated by Duke University Libraries as a standalone facility. Recommend this facility record be reviewed for removal or recategorization during the facility-research phase rather than assigned fabricated IT/MW specifications.

reading:
This row is kept deliberately as a documented data quality problem rather than presented as a working data center, because the registry's policy is to show a bad record and explain it rather than delete it quietly or fill it with invented specifications.

The row names Duke Libraries, the library system of Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, as an operator. The facility attached to it is an OpenStreetMap node called Brandaleone Lab for Data and Visualization, with coordinates on Telecom Drive in Durham. Two separate things are wrong with that pairing. First, the name belongs to a room, not a building. Duke University Libraries publishes the lab's location as the first floor of Bostock Library, inside the space known as the Edge, on Duke's West Campus. It holds nine high performance workstations loaded with Stata, R, Python, MATLAB, Tableau, Adobe Creative Cloud, ArcGIS and QGIS, three laptop docking stations and three Bloomberg financial workstations, and is open to Duke affiliates during Bostock's hours. It is a consultation and analysis room operated by the Libraries' Center for Data and Visualization Sciences. There is no server hall in it. The most likely cause of the mistagging is simply that the name contains the word data, a pattern this registry treats as a reason for extra scrutiny.

Second, the coordinates point somewhere else entirely. Telecom Drive is where Duke's Office of Information Technology telecommunications building sits, a different unit of the university a couple of miles from Bostock. Duke's own public material about that address describes user facing services there, including the DukeCard office and the Technology Engagement Center with its CoLab and 3D printing, and university notices in August 2023 about relocating services after flooding in the building likewise describe those services rather than any machine room. Duke plainly runs central IT infrastructure somewhere, but it publishes no capacity, floor area or power figure for any facility under the Libraries' name, and the Libraries do not operate one.

For completeness, the one large Libraries building that an automated tagger might plausibly mistake for a computing facility is the Duke University Library Service Center at 5 Anson Street in Durham, opened in 2001 and shared with the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. It is a high density physical storage repository with thirty foot shelving, held near 50 degrees Fahrenheit and 30 percent relative humidity, with capacity reported up to fifteen million volumes. That is a book warehouse, not a data center. No IT capacity, square footage or power figure is recorded for this operator, and the row is flagged for recategorization or removal rather than treated as a genuine operator.
